title: Practice essay (45 minutes)
description: One essay of up to 1000 words, written to time, as in an exam. Your answer is submitted when the time is up.
instructions:
Write one essay. You have 45 minutes, including the time to plan your answer.

  • Plan before you write: a few minutes spent on an outline (headings, or a list that you delete later) gives a clearer essay.
  • Use paragraphs. Headings, a table or a labelled drawing can help, but they are not required.
  • The limit is 1000 words; you cannot type more than that. The word count is under the answer box.
  • Write the essay here: as in the real exam, text copied from outside the exam cannot be pasted in.
  • The spelling checker is off, as in most exams. You can switch it on in the menu ☰.
  • When the time is up, your answer is submitted as it is.

questions.title: Blood vessels
questions.text: Compare the structure of arteries, capillaries and veins, and explain how the structure of each type of vessel suits its role in the circulation.
questions.guidance:
What the examiners look for. The question asks for a comparison and for explanation: a good essay is organised around the functions of the vessels, not a list of facts about each one.

  • The general plan of the wall: tunica intima (endothelium on a basement membrane), tunica media (smooth muscle and elastic tissue) and tunica adventitia (connective tissue); how the proportions differ between vessels.
  • Elastic (conducting) arteries such as the aorta: many elastic laminae in the media stretch during systole and recoil during diastole, damping the pressure swings and keeping blood flowing between heartbeats.
  • Muscular (distributing) arteries and arterioles: a thick layer of smooth muscle; arterioles are the main resistance vessels, and changing their radius controls blood pressure and the distribution of flow to the organs (resistance depends steeply on radius).
  • Capillaries: a single layer of endothelial cells on a basement membrane gives the short diffusion distance needed for exchange; their enormous number gives a large total cross-sectional area, so blood flows slowly through them; continuous, fenestrated and sinusoidal capillaries suit different tissues.
  • Veins: thin walls and a large lumen at low pressure; they hold most of the blood volume (capacitance vessels); valves and the skeletal-muscle pump keep blood moving back to the heart.
  • Links between structure and pressure: for example, the tension in a wall rises with pressure and radius (Laplace’s law), which helps to explain why a capillary can have a very thin wall.

A guide to the marks: accurate structure of each type of vessel (8); explanation of how structure suits function (10); comparison rather than separate descriptions (3); organisation and clarity, within the word limit (4).
